subject: English
topic: Grammar mechanics, agreement, parallelism, and modifiers
question: Correct the sentence: "One of the boys are absent today."

options.A: One of the boys is absent today.
options.B: One of the boys were absent today.
options.C: One of the boys have been absent today.
options.D: One of the boy are absent today.

explanation: The subject is singular "One", which governs the singular verb "is".

subject: English
topic: Grammar mechanics, agreement, parallelism, and modifiers
question: Correct: "She is more cleverer than her sister."

options.A: She is cleverer than her sister.
options.B: She is more clever than her sister.
options.C: She is most cleverer than her sister.
options.D: She is clever than her sister.

explanation: Double comparatives ("more cleverer") are grammatically incorrect in standard English.

subject: English
topic: Grammar mechanics, agreement, parallelism, and modifiers
question: Correct: "He gave me many advices."

options.A: He gave me many pieces of advice.
options.B: He gave me many advice.
options.C: He gave me much advices.
options.D: He gave me advices.

explanation: "Advice" is uncountable; plural countable sense uses "pieces of advice".

subject: English
topic: Grammar mechanics, agreement, parallelism, and modifiers
question: Correct: "The scenery of Swat are breathtaking."

options.A: The scenery of Swat is breathtaking.
options.B: The sceneries of Swat are breathtaking.
options.C: The scenery of Swat were breathtaking.
options.D: The sceneries of Swat is breathtaking.

explanation: "Scenery" is an uncountable singular noun requiring "is".

subject: English
topic: Grammar mechanics, agreement, parallelism, and modifiers
question: Correct: "He is senior than me in service."

options.A: He is senior to me in service.
options.B: He is senior from me in service.
options.C: He is senior over me in service.
options.D: He is more senior than me in service.

explanation: Latin comparatives (senior, junior, prior, superior) take the preposition "to".

subject: English
topic: Grammar mechanics, agreement, parallelism, and modifiers
question: Correct: "Neither Ali nor his friends was present."

options.A: Neither Ali nor his friends were present.
options.B: Neither Ali nor his friends is present.
options.C: Neither Ali nor his friends has present.
options.D: Neither Ali nor his friends was not present.

explanation: With "neither...nor", the verb agrees with the closer subject ("friends" -> "were").

subject: English
topic: Grammar mechanics, agreement, parallelism, and modifiers
question: Correct: "I, you and he will travel together."

options.A: You, he and I will travel together.
options.B: He, you and I will travel together.
options.C: I, he and you will travel together.
options.D: You, I and he will travel together.

explanation: For normal polite actions, the order of personal pronouns is Second, Third, First (2-3-1: You, he and I).

subject: English
topic: Grammar mechanics, agreement, parallelism, and modifiers
question: Correct: "Although he worked hard, but he failed."

options.A: Although he worked hard, he failed.
options.B: Although he worked hard, and he failed.
options.C: Although he worked hard, yet but he failed.
options.D: Although he worked hard but failed.

explanation: "Although" and "but" cannot be used together in the same sentence (redundancy).

subject: English
topic: Grammar mechanics, agreement, parallelism, and modifiers
question: Correct: "He is suffering from fever since two days."

options.A: He has been suffering from fever for two days.
options.B: He is suffering from fever for two days.
options.C: He was suffering from fever since two days.
options.D: He has suffered from fever since two days.

explanation: Ongoing duration requires Present Perfect Continuous with "for" ("for two days").

subject: English
topic: Grammar mechanics, agreement, parallelism, and modifiers
question: Correct: "The cattle is grazing in the field."

options.A: The cattle are grazing in the field.
options.B: The cattles are grazing in the field.
options.C: The cattles is grazing in the field.
options.D: The cattle has grazing in the field.

explanation: "Cattle" is always a plural noun and takes the plural verb "are".

subject: English
topic: Grammar mechanics, agreement, parallelism, and modifiers
question: Correct: "Each student must bring their own calculator."

options.A: Each student must bring his or her own calculator.
options.B: Each students must bring their calculator.
options.C: Each student must bring theirs calculator.
options.D: Each student must brought his calculator.

explanation: Singular indefinite distributive "Each student" formally takes singular pronoun "his/her".

subject: English
topic: Grammar mechanics, agreement, parallelism, and modifiers
question: Correct: "Walking down the street, the trees looked beautiful."

options.A: As I was walking down the street, the trees looked beautiful.
options.B: Walking down the street, beautiful were the trees.
options.C: The trees walked down the street beautifully.
options.D: Walking down street, trees looked beauty.

explanation: Fixes the dangling modifier by providing the logical subject ("As I was walking...").

subject: English
topic: Grammar mechanics, agreement, parallelism, and modifiers
question: Correct: "He did not know nothing about the plan."

options.A: He did not know anything about the plan.
options.B: He did not know no thing about the plan.
options.C: He knew not nothing about the plan.
options.D: He did know nothing not about the plan.

explanation: Eliminates the double negative error ("did not know anything").

subject: English
topic: Grammar mechanics, agreement, parallelism, and modifiers
question: Correct: "She is good in English."

options.A: She is good at English.
options.B: She is good with English.
options.C: She is good on English.
options.D: She is good for English.

explanation: The standard dependent preposition for proficiency is "good at".

subject: English
topic: Grammar mechanics, agreement, parallelism, and modifiers
question: Correct: "He prevented me to go there."

options.A: He prevented me from going there.
options.B: He prevented me going there.
options.C: He prevented me to going there.
options.D: He prevented me for going there.

explanation: "Prevent" is idiomatically followed by "from + gerund".

subject: English
topic: Grammar mechanics, agreement, parallelism, and modifiers
question: Correct: "He is guilty for theft."

options.A: He is guilty of theft.
options.B: He is guilty with theft.
options.C: He is guilty in theft.
options.D: He is guilty to theft.

explanation: "Guilty" takes the fixed preposition "of".

subject: English
topic: Grammar mechanics, agreement, parallelism, and modifiers
question: Correct: "I prefer milk than tea."

options.A: I prefer milk to tea.
options.B: I prefer milk over tea.
options.C: I prefer milk more than tea.
options.D: I prefer milk against tea.

explanation: The verb "prefer" is always followed by "to", not "than".

subject: English
topic: Grammar mechanics, agreement, parallelism, and modifiers
question: Correct: "This cloth is superior than that."

options.A: This cloth is superior to that.
options.B: This cloth is superior from that.
options.C: This cloth is more superior than that.
options.D: This cloth is superior over that.

explanation: "Superior" takes "to".

subject: English
topic: Grammar mechanics, agreement, parallelism, and modifiers
question: Correct: "Ten miles are a long distance to walk."

options.A: Ten miles is a long distance to walk.
options.B: Ten miles were a long distance to walk.
options.C: Ten miles have been a long distance to walk.
options.D: Ten miles are long distances to walk.

explanation: A specific distance or quantity viewed as a single unit takes a singular verb ("is").

subject: English
topic: Grammar mechanics, agreement, parallelism, and modifiers
question: Correct: "Mathematics are a difficult subject for many."

options.A: Mathematics is a difficult subject for many.
options.B: Mathematics were a difficult subject for many.
options.C: Mathematic is a difficult subject for many.
options.D: Mathematics have been a difficult subject.

explanation: Academic subjects ending in -s (Mathematics, Physics) take a singular verb.

subject: English
topic: Grammar mechanics, agreement, parallelism, and modifiers
question: Correct: "He died from malaria."

options.A: He died of malaria.
options.B: He died with malaria.
options.C: He died by malaria.
options.D: He died through malaria.

explanation: One dies "of" a disease, not "from" or "by".

subject: English
topic: Grammar mechanics, agreement, parallelism, and modifiers
question: Correct: "Unless you do not work hard, you will fail."

options.A: Unless you work hard, you will fail.
options.B: Unless you did not work hard, you will fail.
options.C: Unless you will work hard, you will fail.
options.D: Unless you do work hard, you will not fail.

explanation: "Unless" already contains the negative meaning; adding "do not" is a double negative.

subject: English
topic: Grammar mechanics, agreement, parallelism, and modifiers
question: Correct: "He asked me that what my name was."

options.A: He asked me what my name was.
options.B: He asked me that what was my name.
options.C: He asked me what was my name.
options.D: He asked that my name what was.

explanation: In indirect WH-questions, conjunction "that" must be omitted.

subject: English
topic: Grammar mechanics, agreement, parallelism, and modifiers
question: Correct: "Between you and I, this secret must be kept."

options.A: Between you and me, this secret must be kept.
options.B: Between you and myself, this secret must be kept.
options.C: Between he and I, this secret must be kept.
options.D: Between you and mine, this secret must be kept.

explanation: Prepositions require objective case pronouns ("Between you and me").

subject: English
topic: Grammar mechanics, agreement, parallelism, and modifiers
question: Correct: "He ordered for a cup of tea."

options.A: He ordered a cup of tea.
options.B: He ordered with a cup of tea.
options.C: He ordered to a cup of tea.
options.D: He ordered about a cup of tea.

explanation: As a transitive verb, "ordered" directly takes its object without "for".

subject: English
topic: Grammar mechanics, agreement, parallelism, and modifiers
question: Correct: "She resembles to her mother."

options.A: She resembles her mother.
options.B: She resembles with her mother.
options.C: She resembles like her mother.
options.D: She resembles of her mother.

explanation: "Resemble" is a transitive verb and takes no preposition.

subject: English
topic: Grammar mechanics, agreement, parallelism, and modifiers
question: Correct: "He entered into the room quietly."

options.A: He entered the room quietly.
options.B: He entered inside the room quietly.
options.C: He entered to the room quietly.
options.D: He entered within the room quietly.

explanation: "Enter" meaning physical entry takes no preposition ("entered the room").

subject: English
topic: Grammar mechanics, agreement, parallelism, and modifiers
question: Correct: "I, you and he committed a blunder."

options.A: I, you and he committed a blunder.
options.B: You, he and I committed a blunder.
options.C: He, you and I committed a blunder.
options.D: You, I and he committed a blunder.

explanation: When confessing a mistake/blame, the order is First, Second, Third (1-2-3: I, you and he).

subject: English
topic: Grammar mechanics, agreement, parallelism, and modifiers
question: Correct: "Let you and I solve this problem."

options.A: Let you and me solve this problem.
options.B: Let you and myself solve this problem.
options.C: Let he and I solve this problem.
options.D: Let you and we solve this problem.

explanation: "Let" is followed by objective case pronouns ("you and me").

subject: English
topic: Grammar mechanics, agreement, parallelism, and modifiers
question: Correct: "No less than fifty students were present."

options.A: No fewer than fifty students were present.
options.B: No lesser than fifty students were present.
options.C: Not less than fifty students were present.
options.D: No few than fifty students were present.

explanation: "Fewer" is used for countable nouns ("fifty students"), whereas "less" is for uncountable.

subject: English
topic: Grammar mechanics, agreement, parallelism, and modifiers
question: Correct: "He is both intelligent as well as hardworking."

options.A: He is both intelligent and hardworking.
options.B: He is both intelligent also hardworking.
options.C: He is both intelligent but hardworking.
options.D: He is both intelligent with hardworking.

explanation: The correlative conjunction "both" is strictly paired with "and".

subject: English
topic: Grammar mechanics, agreement, parallelism, and modifiers
question: Correct: "I will not go lest you should not accompany me."

options.A: I will not go lest you should accompany me.
options.B: I will not go lest you accompany me not.
options.C: I will not go lest you will accompany me.
options.D: I will not go lest you do not accompany me.

explanation: "Lest" is already negative and takes "should" without an extra "not".

subject: English
topic: Grammar mechanics, agreement, parallelism, and modifiers
question: Correct: "She sings good."

options.A: She sings well.
options.B: She sings bestly.
options.C: She sings goodly.
options.D: She sings goodness.

explanation: "Well" is the adverb modifying the verb "sings"; "good" is an adjective.

subject: English
topic: Grammar mechanics, agreement, parallelism, and modifiers
question: Correct: "The committee have passed the resolution unanimously."

options.A: The committee has passed the resolution unanimously.
options.B: The committee have been passed the resolution.
options.C: The committee were passed the resolution.
options.D: The committees has passed the resolution.

explanation: A collective noun acting as a single unanimous entity takes a singular verb ("has").

subject: English
topic: Grammar mechanics, agreement, parallelism, and modifiers
question: Correct: "He returned back from Karachi yesterday."

options.A: He returned from Karachi yesterday.
options.B: He returned back to Karachi yesterday.
options.C: He has returned back from Karachi.
options.D: He return back from Karachi.

explanation: "Returned back" is a redundant tautology; "returned" suffices.

subject: English
topic: Grammar mechanics, agreement, parallelism, and modifiers
question: Correct: "She is too happy to see you."

options.A: She is very happy to see you.
options.B: She is much happy to see you.
options.C: She is so happy to see you.
options.D: She is enough happy to see you.

explanation: "Too" has an excessively negative connotation; "very happy" is correct.

subject: English
topic: Grammar mechanics, agreement, parallelism, and modifiers
question: Correct: "He gave me a five-rupees note."

options.A: He gave me a five-rupee note.
options.B: He gave me a five-rupee notes.
options.C: He gave me five-rupees notes.
options.D: He gave me a five-rupees notes.

explanation: Hyphenated compound adjectives of quantity remain singular ("five-rupee note").

subject: English
topic: Grammar mechanics, agreement, parallelism, and modifiers
question: Correct: "I congratulated him for his success."

options.A: I congratulated him on his success.
options.B: I congratulated him at his success.
options.C: I congratulated him with his success.
options.D: I congratulated him to his success.

explanation: "Congratulate" takes the fixed preposition "on".

subject: English
topic: Grammar mechanics, agreement, parallelism, and modifiers
question: Correct: "He is confident to win the match."

options.A: He is confident of winning the match.
options.B: He is confident for winning the match.
options.C: He is confident in win the match.
options.D: He is confident with winning.

explanation: "Confident" is followed by "of + gerund".

subject: English
topic: Grammar mechanics, agreement, parallelism, and modifiers
question: Correct: "None of the two boys came."

options.A: Neither of the two boys came.
options.B: No one of the two boys came.
options.C: Not any of the two boys came.
options.D: Neither of the two boy came.

explanation: "Neither" is used when referring to two persons; "none" is for three or more.

subject: English
topic: Grammar mechanics, agreement, parallelism, and modifiers
question: Identify the grammatically correct sentence:

options.A: Neither the captain nor the players were satisfied with the decision.
options.B: Neither the captain nor the players was satisfied with the decision.
options.C: Neither the captain or the players were satisfied with the decision.
options.D: Neither the captain nor the players has been satisfied with the decision.

explanation: With "neither...nor", the verb agrees with the nearer subject ("players" -> plural verb "were").

subject: English
topic: Grammar mechanics, agreement, parallelism, and modifiers
question: Correct the error: "He is more taller than his elder brother."

options.A: He is taller than his elder brother.
options.B: He is most taller than his elder brother.
options.C: He is more tall than his elder brother.
options.D: He is taller then his elder brother.

explanation: "More taller" is an incorrect double comparative; "taller" is sufficient.

subject: English
topic: Grammar mechanics, agreement, parallelism, and modifiers
question: Identify the correct sentence containing parallel structure:

options.A: She enjoys reading historical novels, playing the piano, and swimming.
options.B: She enjoys reading historical novels, to play the piano, and swimming.
options.C: She enjoys reading historical novels, piano playing, and to swim.
options.D: She enjoys to read novels, playing the piano, and swim.

explanation: All three coordinate elements must share the same grammatical form (gerunds: reading, playing, swimming).

subject: English
topic: Grammar mechanics, agreement, parallelism, and modifiers
question: Choose the correct version of the sentence: "One of the boys have forgotten his notebook."

options.A: One of the boys has forgotten his notebook.
options.B: One of the boys have forgotten their notebook.
options.C: One of the boy has forgotten his notebook.
options.D: One of the boys had forgot their notebook.

explanation: The subject is "One" (singular), so it takes the singular verb "has" and singular pronoun "his".

subject: English
topic: Grammar mechanics, agreement, parallelism, and modifiers
question: Identify the sentence that fixes the dangling modifier: "Walking through the orchard, the apples caught my attention."

options.A: While I was walking through the orchard, the apples caught my attention.
options.B: Walking through the orchard, my attention was caught by apples.
options.C: Walking through the orchard, the apples were seen by me.
options.D: Having walked through the orchard, apples caught my eye.

explanation: The introductory participle must logically modify the agent ("I"), not "the apples".

subject: English
topic: Grammar mechanics, agreement, parallelism, and modifiers
question: Correct the error in: "He did not know nothing about the upcoming examination."

options.A: He did not know anything about the upcoming examination.
options.B: He did know nothing about the upcoming examination.
options.C: He did not know no thing about the upcoming examination.
options.D: He does not know nothing about the upcoming examination.

explanation: "Did not know nothing" is an incorrect double negative. Use "anything" with "not".

subject: English
topic: Grammar mechanics, agreement, parallelism, and modifiers
question: Choose the correct sentence:

options.A: Scarcely had he reached the station when the train departed.
options.B: Scarcely had he reached the station than the train departed.
options.C: Scarcely had he reached the station then the train departed.
options.D: Scarcely he had reached the station when the train departed.

explanation: "Scarcely...when" is the correct correlative pair with inverted subject-auxiliary order ("had he reached").

subject: English
topic: Grammar mechanics, agreement, parallelism, and modifiers
question: Select the grammatically accurate sentence:

options.A: The furniture in this showroom is made of solid oak.
options.B: The furnitures in this showroom are made of solid oak.
options.C: The furnitures in this showroom is made of solid oak.
options.D: The furniture in this showroom are made of solid oak.

explanation: "Furniture" is an uncountable noun that takes a singular verb and has no plural form with -s.

subject: English
topic: Grammar mechanics, agreement, parallelism, and modifiers
question: Choose the correct sentence regarding pronoun case:

options.A: Between you and me, the new proposal seems impracticable.
options.B: Between you and I, the new proposal seems impracticable.
options.C: Between you and myself, the new proposal seems impracticable.
options.D: Between he and I, the new proposal seems impracticable.

explanation: Prepositions (like "Between") take objective case pronouns ("you and me").

subject: English
topic: Grammar mechanics, agreement, parallelism, and modifiers
question: Identify the sentence free of punctuation and agreement errors:

options.A: Ten kilometers is a considerable distance to walk on foot.
options.B: Ten kilometers are a considerable distance to walk on foot.
options.C: Ten kilometer is a considerable distance to walk on foot.
options.D: Ten kilometers are considerable distances to walk on foot.

explanation: A plural quantity of distance, time, or money regarded as a single unit takes a singular verb ("is").
